title: Unconditional containment of unambiguous probabilistic automata
formal: Is quantitative containment decidable when the left automaton \(A\) is unambiguous and the right automaton \(B\) is finitely ambiguous? In other words, does a single unconditional terminating algorithm decide \(\forall w\in\Sigma^{*},\ p_A(w)\leq p_B(w)\) for every promised pair of rational probabilistic automata as defined below? This selects the direction of bounded-ambiguity containment whose known decidability proof uses Schanuel’s conjecture; the reverse direction is already decidable unconditionally.
why: This asks whether a basic exact comparison between small stochastic models can be decided from a finite bound on accepting behavior, without a conjecture in transcendental number theory. The asymmetry between one probability product and a bounded sum isolates the unresolved arithmetic obstacle in an otherwise effective verification setting.
status_note: The 2021 primary journal theorem remains conditional for this direction, and the 2021 seminar question, published in 2022, specifically asks to remove that assumption. Bounded source and later-literature checks on 13 September 2026 found no unconditional decision theorem. This does not establish exhaustive present-day openness.

progress.text: The journal version proves the finitely-ambiguous-left direction unconditionally and retains Schanuel’s conjecture for the unambiguous-left direction.
The published seminar report asks for the conjectural assumption to be removed.

sentences: A probabilistic automaton assigns each finite word an acceptance probability.
The left automaton here has at most one positive accepting run per word, while the right one has a fixed finite bound on that number.
The task is to decide whether the left probability is at most the right probability for every word, with exact comparison and no numerical gap promise.
The known result for this direction assumes Schanuel’s conjecture; the reversed direction already has an unconditional algorithm.
An accepted answer proves decidability or undecidability in Lean without retaining the conjectural arithmetic assumption.

definitions: A probabilistic automaton is \(A=(\Sigma,Q,\delta,\iota,F)\), with a finite nonempty alphabet \(\Sigma\), a finite nonempty state set \(Q\), accepting states \(F\subseteq Q\), nonnegative rational initial weights \(\iota(q)\) satisfying \(\sum_q\iota(q)\leq1\), and nonnegative rational transition weights \(\delta(q,a,p)\) satisfying \(\sum_p\delta(q,a,p)\leq1\) for each state \(q\) and letter \(a\). Missing probability mass is lost to rejection. There are no epsilon transitions. The input lists the states, alphabet, initial weights, accepting states and all nonzero transitions; rational numerators and positive denominators use binary notation.

For \(w=a_1\cdots a_m\), a positive accepting run is a state sequence \(q_0,\ldots,q_m\) with \(q_m\in F\) and \(\iota(q_0)\prod_{i=1}^{m}\delta(q_{i-1},a_i,q_i)>0\). Its weight is this product. Let \(p_A(w)\) be the sum of these weights. In particular \(p_A(\varepsilon)=\sum_{q\in F}\iota(q)\). Zero-weight transitions do not create runs; identical state-and-letter transitions are represented by one weight.

Unambiguous means at most one positive accepting run for each word. Finitely ambiguous means that there exists one integer \(K\geq0\), depending on the automaton but independent of the word and its length, such that every word has at most \(K\) positive accepting runs. This bound need not be supplied. Every finite word has finitely many runs even without the promise; a uniform bound over all words is the essential restriction.

Quantitative containment means exact pointwise comparison \(p_A(w)\leq p_B(w)\) for every finite word \(w\in\Sigma^{*}\), including the empty word. There is no cutpoint, approximation tolerance, isolated-gap promise, or bounded word length.

Decidability asks for one deterministic Turing machine on the finite descriptions, halting on every input string and outputting a bit. On each pair satisfying the stated structural promises, the bit must be 1 precisely for quantitative containment; outside the promise either bit is permitted. There is no time bound, oracle or unproved mathematical assumption in the requested result.
answer_criterion: A complete Lean-checked proof of an unconditional decision algorithm for the stated promise problem, or a Lean-checked proof that no such algorithm exists. A proof conditional on Schanuel’s conjecture or on the decidability of real exponentiation is not sufficient. A procedure that only terminates when a violating word exists is not a decider.

context_blocks.text: The seminar question asks whether the conjectural arithmetic assumption can be removed from bounded-ambiguity probabilistic containment. The precise benchmark fixes the left-unambiguous, right-finitely-ambiguous case so that it targets the remaining conditional direction of the primary theorem.

The journal paper distinguishes the two directions. Proposition 16 gives an unconditional decision procedure when the left side is finitely ambiguous and the right side unambiguous. Theorem 17 handles the converse under Schanuel’s conjecture through the decidability of the first-order real field with exponentiation.

Allowing finite ambiguity on both sides is a more general question, recorded separately in TCS-3863. Its decidability would imply a positive answer here; undecidability here would imply undecidability for that generalization.

statement_review.notes: Interpreted the seminar’s broad bounded-ambiguity wording through the primary theorem: selected the still-conditional unambiguous-left direction and labeled that specification. Distinguished quantitative pointwise containment from cutpoint language inclusion, and the unconditional reverse direction from the target. Defined rational subprobability weights, positive-run ambiguity and a uniform word-independent bound. Linked, without merging, the genuinely broader two-finitely-ambiguous question.
